e-616.knowledge_point: Finding the Velocity Vector of a Particle Moving in Two Dimensions
e-616.problem:
The position vector $\mathbf{r}$ of a particle $P$ relative to a fixed origin $O$ at time $t > 0$ is given by

$$
\mathbf{r} = \langle 3t^3, 2t^2\rangle.
$$

Calculate the velocity vector $\mathbf{v}.$
e-616.worked_solution:
The particle's velocity vector is given by the derivative of its position vector:

$$
\begin{aligned}v & =\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}t} \\  & =⟨\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t},\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(3{t}^{3}),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2{t}^{2})⟩ \\  & =⟨9{t}^{2},\,4t⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

e-617.knowledge_point: Calculating the Velocity Vector of a Particle Moving in Two Dimensions at a Given Time
e-617.problem:
The position vector $\mathbf{r}$ of a particle $P$ (relative to a fixed origin $O$) at time $t > 0$ is given by

$$
\mathbf{r} = \langle 12t, 2t^3\rangle.
$$

Calculate the velocity vector $\mathbf{v}$ at time $t=1.$
e-617.worked_solution:
The particle's velocity vector is given by the derivative of its position vector:

$$
\begin{aligned}v & =\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}t} \\  & =⟨\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t},\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(12t),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2{t}^{3})⟩ \\  & =⟨12,6{t}^{2}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

To find the velocity when $t=1$, we substitute into the above:

$$
\begin{aligned}v(1) & =⟨12,6(1)^{2}⟩ \\  & =⟨12,6⟩\end{aligned}
$$

e-618.knowledge_point: Calculating the Speed of a Particle at a Given Time
e-618.problem:
The position vector $\mathbf{r}$ of a particle $P$ relative to a fixed origin $O$ at time $t > 0$ is given by

$$
\mathbf{r} = \langle 6t^2+2, 2t^3\rangle.
$$

Calculate the speed of the particle at time $t=2.$
e-618.worked_solution:
First, we calculate the velocity vector $\mathbf{v}.$ Differentiating the position vector, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}v & =\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}t} \\  & =⟨\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t},\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(6{t}^{2}+2),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2{t}^{3})⟩ \\  & =⟨12t,6{t}^{2}⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

To find the velocity when $t=2$, we substitute into the above:

$$
\begin{aligned}v(2) & =⟨12(2),6(2)^{2}⟩ \\  & =⟨24,24⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

To find the speed at $t=2$ we calculate the magnitude of $\mathbf{v}(2),$ and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}|v(2)| & =\sqrt{{24}^{2}+{24}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{2({24}^{2})} \\  & =24\sqrt{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

So, the speed when $t=2$ is $24\sqrt{2}\approx 33.94$ to two decimal places.

e-619.knowledge_point: Calculating the Times at Which a Particle Is Stationary
e-619.problem:
A particle $P$ moves in the $x$-$y$ plane (relative to a fixed origin $O$) with position vector

$$
\mathbf{r} = \langle t^2-2t, t^3-3t \rangle, \quad t\in[0,\infty).
$$

Calculate the times at which the particle is stationary.
e-619.worked_solution:
First, we calculate the velocity vector $\mathbf{v}.$ Differentiating the position vector, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}v & =\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}t} \\  & =⟨\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t},\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{2}-2t),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{3}-3t)⟩ \\  & =⟨2t-2,\,3{t}^{2}-3⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

The particle is stationary when its velocity is zero. This gives,

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =0 \\ ⟨2t-2,3{t}^{2}-3⟩ & =⟨0,0⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

So we need

$$
\begin{aligned}2t-2 & =0\,⇒\,t=1, \\ 3{t}^{2}-3 & =0\,⇒\,t=\pm 1.\end{aligned}
$$

Note that $t=-1$ is outside of the domain of $t,$ so we discard it. 

The solution $t=1$ is the only solution that satisfies both equations, so this is the only time when the object is stationary.

The position vector r of a particle P (relative to a fixed origin O) at time t is given by r=⟨et2−1,2−5t⟩,t>0. Calculate the velocity vector v.

a
v=⟨et2−1,2⟩
b
v=⟨2tet2−1,2⟩
c
v=⟨tet2−1,−5⟩
d
v=⟨et2−1,−5⟩
e

decision.explanation: Differentiate each component. The chain rule gives d(e^{t^2-1})/dt=2te^{t^2-1}, and d(2-5t)/dt=-5. Therefore option e is correct.

The position vector $r$ of a particle $P$ (relative to a fixed origin $O$) at time $t$ is given by

$$
r=⟨{e}^{{t}^{2}-1},2-5t⟩,\,t>0.

Calculate the velocity vector $v.$

$$

$$

Question 2
?

The position vector r of a particle P (relative to a fixed origin O) at time t is given by r=⟨et2−1,2−5t⟩,t>0. Calculate the velocity vector v.

a
v=⟨et2−1,2⟩
b
v=⟨2tet2−1,2⟩
c
v=⟨tet2−1,−5⟩
d
v=⟨et2−1,−5⟩
e
v=⟨2tet2−1,−5⟩
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The particle's velocity vector is given by the derivative of its position vector: v=drdt=⟨dxdt,dydt⟩=⟨ddt(et2−1),ddt(2−5t)⟩=⟨2tet2−1,−5⟩

content.knowledge_point: Finding the Velocity Vector of a Particle Moving in Two Dimensions
content.problem:
The position vector $r$ of a particle $P$ (relative to a fixed origin $O$) at time $t$ is given by

$$
r=⟨{e}^{{t}^{2}-1},2-5t⟩,\,t>0.
$$

Calculate the velocity vector $v.$
content.worked_solution:
The particle's velocity vector is given by the derivative of its position vector:

$$
\begin{aligned}v & =\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}t} \\  & =⟨\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t},\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({e}^{{t}^{2}-1}),\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2-5t)⟩ \\  & =⟨2t{e}^{{t}^{2}-1},-5⟩\end{aligned}
$$

before.html:
Question 3
?

The position vector r of a particle P (relative to a fixed origin O) at time t is given by r=⟨1−3t2,sin⁡(2t+1)⟩,t>0. Calculate the velocity vector v.

a
v=⟨−6,cos⁡(2t+1)⟩
b
v=⟨−6t,−2cos⁡(2t+1)⟩
c
v=⟨−6t,2cos⁡(2t+1)⟩
d
v=⟨−6t,−cos⁡(2t+1)⟩
e
v=⟨−6,2cos⁡(2t+1)⟩
Submit

decision.explanation: Velocity is the derivative of position. Differentiating 1-3t^2 gives -6t; the chain rule gives the derivative of sin(2t+1) as 2cos(2t+1). Thus option c is correct.

after.name: Question 3
after.problem:
The position vector $r$ of a particle $P$ (relative to a fixed origin $O$) at time $t$ is given by

$$
r=⟨1-3{t}^{2},\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t+1)⟩,\,t>0.
$$

Calculate the velocity vector $v.$
after.worked_solution:
The particle's velocity vector is given by the derivative of its position vector:

$$
\begin{aligned}v & =\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}t} \\  & =⟨\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t},\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(1-3{t}^{2}),\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t+1))⟩ \\  & =⟨-6t,2\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t+1)⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Question 3

The position vector r of a particle P (relative to a fixed origin O) at time t is given by r=⟨1−3t2,sin⁡(2t+1)⟩,t>0. Calculate the velocity vector v.

a
v=⟨−6,cos⁡(2t+1)⟩
b
v=⟨−6t,−2cos⁡(2t+1)⟩
c
v=⟨−6t,2cos⁡(2t+1)⟩
d
v=⟨−6t,−cos⁡(2t+1)⟩
e
v=⟨−6,2cos⁡(2t+1)⟩
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

The particle's velocity vector is given by the derivative of its position vector: v=drdt=⟨dxdt,dydt⟩=⟨ddt(1−3t2),ddt(sin⁡(2t+1))⟩=⟨−6t,2cos⁡(2t+1)⟩

verification.explanation: The worked solution confirms option c: differentiating 1-3t^2 gives -6t, and the chain rule gives d(sin(2t+1))/dt=2cos(2t+1). The deliberately submitted option a is incorrect.

content.knowledge_point: Finding the Velocity Vector of a Particle Moving in Two Dimensions
content.problem:
The position vector $r$ of a particle $P$ (relative to a fixed origin $O$) at time $t$ is given by

$$
r=⟨1-3{t}^{2},\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t+1)⟩,\,t>0.
$$

Calculate the velocity vector $v.$
content.worked_solution:
The particle's velocity vector is given by the derivative of its position vector:

$$
\begin{aligned}v & =\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}t} \\  & =⟨\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t},\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(1-3{t}^{2}),\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t+1))⟩ \\  & =⟨-6t,2\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t+1)⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Question 4
?

A particle P is moving in the x-y plane. Its position vector relative to a fixed origin O is given by r=⟨t3/2+4t2,11t−1⟩,t>0. Calculate the velocity vector v.

a
v=⟨32t+4t,10⟩
b
v=⟨t+4t,11⟩
c
v=⟨32t3/2+8t2,11t⟩
d
v=⟨32t+8t,11⟩
e
v=⟨t+4t,11t⟩
Submit

decision.explanation: Differentiate each component: d(t^{3/2}+4t^2)/dt=(3/2)√t+8t and d(11t-1)/dt=11. Therefore option d is correct.

after.name: Question 4
after.problem:
A particle $P$ is moving in the $x$-$y$ plane. Its position vector relative to a fixed origin $O$ is given by

$$
r=⟨{t}^{3/2}+4{t}^{2},\,11t-1⟩,\,t>0.
$$

Calculate the velocity vector $v.$
after.worked_solution:
The particle's velocity vector is given by the derivative of its position vector:

$$
\begin{aligned}v & =\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}t} \\  & =⟨\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t},\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{3/2}+4{t}^{2}),\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(11t-1)⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{3}{2}\sqrt{t}+8t,\,11⟩\end{aligned}
$$

after.html:
Question 4
?

A particle P is moving in the x-y plane. Its position vector relative to a fixed origin O is given by r=⟨t3/2+4t2,11t−1⟩,t>0. Calculate the velocity vector v.

a
v=⟨32t+4t,10⟩
b
v=⟨t+4t,11⟩
c
v=⟨32t3/2+8t2,11t⟩
d
v=⟨32t+8t,11⟩
e
v=⟨t+4t,11t⟩
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The particle's velocity vector is given by the derivative of its position vector: v=drdt=⟨dxdt,dydt⟩=⟨ddt(t3/2+4t2),ddt(11t−1)⟩=⟨32t+8t,11⟩

content.knowledge_point: Finding the Velocity Vector of a Particle Moving in Two Dimensions
content.problem:
A particle $P$ is moving in the $x$-$y$ plane. Its position vector relative to a fixed origin $O$ is given by

$$
r=⟨{t}^{3/2}+4{t}^{2},\,11t-1⟩,\,t>0.
$$

Calculate the velocity vector $v.$
content.worked_solution:
The particle's velocity vector is given by the derivative of its position vector:

$$
\begin{aligned}v & =\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}t} \\  & =⟨\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t},\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{3/2}+4{t}^{2}),\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(11t-1)⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{3}{2}\sqrt{t}+8t,\,11⟩\end{aligned}
$$

decision.explanation: Differentiate before substituting t=2. The first component is -7/(t+1)^2, giving -7/9. By the quotient rule, the second is 5(1-t^2)/(t^2+1)^2, giving -15/25=-3/5.

after.name: Question 6
after.problem:
The position vector $r$ of a particle $P$ (relative to a fixed origin $O$) at time $t$ is given by

$$
r=⟨\frac{7}{t+1},\,\frac{5t}{{t}^{2}+1}⟩,\,t>0.
$$

Calculate the components of the velocity vector $v$ at time $t=2.$ Do not round the answers.

$v(2)=⟨${{field-1}},
{{field-2}}$⟩$
after.worked_solution:
The particle's velocity vector is given by the derivative of its position vector:

$$
\begin{aligned}v & =\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}t} \\  & =⟨\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t},\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{7}{t+1}),\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{5t}{{t}^{2}+1})⟩ \\  & =⟨-\frac{7}{(t+1)^{2}},\frac{5-5{t}^{2}}{({t}^{2}+1)^{2}}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Question 8

The position vector r of a particle P (relative to a fixed origin O) at time t is given by r=⟨tcos⁡t,t+sin⁡t⟩,t>0. Calculate the velocity vector v at time t=π2.

a
v(π2)=⟨0,0⟩
b
v(π2)=⟨−π2,1⟩
c
v(π2)=⟨1,−1⟩
d
v(π2)=⟨−π,1⟩
e
v(π2)=⟨π2,1⟩
Submit

decision.explanation: The product rule gives v(t)=⟨cos(t)-t sin(t),1+cos(t)⟩. At t=π/2, cos(t)=0 and sin(t)=1, so v(π/2)=⟨-π/2,1⟩, matching option b.

after.problem:
The position vector $r$ of a particle $P$ (relative to a fixed origin $O$) at time $t$ is given by

$$
r=⟨t\operatorname{cos}⁡t,t+\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩,\,t>0.
$$

Calculate the velocity vector $v$ at time $t=\frac{\pi }{2}.$
after.worked_solution:
The particle's velocity vector is given by the derivative of its position vector:

$$
\begin{aligned}v & =\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}t} \\  & =⟨\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t},\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t\operatorname{cos}⁡t),\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t+\operatorname{sin}⁡t)⟩ \\  & =⟨\operatorname{cos}⁡t-t\operatorname{sin}⁡t,1+\operatorname{cos}⁡t⟩\end{aligned}
$$

To find the velocity when $t=\frac{\pi }{2},$ we substitute into the above:

$$
\begin{aligned}v(\frac{\pi }{2}) & =⟨\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2})-(\frac{\pi }{2})\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2}),1+\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2})⟩ \\  & =⟨0-(\frac{\pi }{2})(1),1+(0)⟩ \\  & =⟨-\frac{\pi }{2},\,1⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Question 8
?

The position vector r of a particle P (relative to a fixed origin O) at time t is given by r=⟨tcos⁡t,t+sin⁡t⟩,t>0. Calculate the velocity vector v at time t=π2.

a
v(π2)=⟨0,0⟩
b
v(π2)=⟨−π2,1⟩
c
v(π2)=⟨1,−1⟩
d
v(π2)=⟨−π,1⟩
e
v(π2)=⟨π2,1⟩
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The particle's velocity vector is given by the derivative of its position vector: v=drdt=⟨dxdt,dydt⟩=⟨ddt(tcos⁡t),ddt(t+sin⁡t)⟩=⟨cos⁡t−tsin⁡t,1+cos⁡t⟩

To find the velocity when t=π2, we substitute into the above: v(π2)=⟨cos⁡(π2)−(π2)sin⁡(π2),1+cos⁡(π2)⟩=⟨0−(π2)(1),1+(0)⟩=⟨−π2,1⟩

content.problem:
The position vector $r$ of a particle $P$ (relative to a fixed origin $O$) at time $t$ is given by

$$
r=⟨t\operatorname{cos}⁡t,t+\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩,\,t>0.
$$

Calculate the velocity vector $v$ at time $t=\frac{\pi }{2}.$
content.worked_solution:
The particle's velocity vector is given by the derivative of its position vector:

$$
\begin{aligned}v & =\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}t} \\  & =⟨\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t},\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t\operatorname{cos}⁡t),\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t+\operatorname{sin}⁡t)⟩ \\  & =⟨\operatorname{cos}⁡t-t\operatorname{sin}⁡t,1+\operatorname{cos}⁡t⟩\end{aligned}
$$

To find the velocity when $t=\frac{\pi }{2},$ we substitute into the above:

$$
\begin{aligned}v(\frac{\pi }{2}) & =⟨\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2})-(\frac{\pi }{2})\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2}),1+\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2})⟩ \\  & =⟨0-(\frac{\pi }{2})(1),1+(0)⟩ \\  & =⟨-\frac{\pi }{2},\,1⟩\end{aligned}
$$

$$

Question 10
?

The position vector r of a particle P (relative to a fixed origin O) at time t is given by r=⟨6t−1,3t+1⟩,t>0. Calculate the velocity vector v at time t=1.

a
v(1)=⟨6,9ln⁡3⟩
b
v(1)=⟨5,9⟩
c
v(1)=⟨6,ln⁡3⟩
d
v(1)=⟨6,3ln⁡3⟩
e
v(1)=⟨5,9ln⁡3⟩
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The particle's velocity vector is given by the derivative of its position vector: v=drdt=⟨dxdt,dydt⟩=⟨ddt(6t−1),ddt(3t+1)⟩=⟨6,3t+1ln⁡3⟩

To find the velocity when t=1, we substitute into the above: v(1)=⟨6,31+1ln⁡3⟩=⟨6,32ln⁡3⟩=⟨6,9ln⁡3⟩

content.knowledge_point: Calculating the Velocity Vector of a Particle Moving in Two Dimensions at a Given Time
content.problem:
The position vector $r$ of a particle $P$ (relative to a fixed origin $O$) at time $t$ is given by

$$
r=⟨6t-1,{3}^{t+1}⟩,\,t>0.
$$

Calculate the velocity vector $v$ at time $t=1.$
content.worked_solution:
The particle's velocity vector is given by the derivative of its position vector:

$$
\begin{aligned}v & =\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}t} \\  & =⟨\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t},\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(6t-1),\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({3}^{t+1})⟩ \\  & =⟨6,{3}^{t+1}\operatorname{ln}⁡3⟩\end{aligned}
$$

To find the velocity when $t=1,$ we substitute into the above:

$$
\begin{aligned}v(1) & =⟨6,{3}^{1+1}\operatorname{ln}⁡3⟩ \\  & =⟨6,{3}^{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡3⟩ \\  & =⟨6,9\operatorname{ln}⁡3⟩\end{aligned}
$$

The position vector r of a particle P (relative to a fixed origin O) at time t is given by r=⟨t2ln⁡t,2t2+9⟩,t>0. Calculate the speed of the particle at time t=e.

a
5e
b
7e
c
5e5
d
5e
e
55e
Submit

decision.explanation: The product rule gives v(t)=⟨2t ln(t)+t,4t⟩. Since ln(e)=1, v(e)=⟨3e,4e⟩. The speed is √((3e)²+(4e)²)=5e, so option a is correct.

after.name: Question 11
after.problem:
The position vector $r$ of a particle $P$ (relative to a fixed origin $O$) at time $t$ is given by

$$
r=⟨{t}^{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡t,\,2{t}^{2}+9⟩,\,t>0.
$$

Calculate the speed of the particle at time $t=e.$
after.worked_solution:
First, we calculate the velocity vector $v.$ Differentiating the position vector, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}v & =\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}t} \\  & =⟨\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t},\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡t),\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2{t}^{2}+9)⟩ \\  & =⟨2t\operatorname{ln}⁡t+t,4t⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

To find the velocity when $t=e,$ we substitute in the above:

$$
\begin{aligned}v(e) & =⟨2e\operatorname{ln}⁡e+e,4e⟩ \\  & =⟨3e,4e⟩\end{aligned}
$$

To find the speed at $t=e$ we calculate the magnitude of $v(e),$ and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}|v(e)| & =\sqrt{(3e)^{2}+(4e)^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{25{e}^{2}} \\  & =5e.\end{aligned}
$$

The position vector r of a particle P (relative to a fixed origin O) at time t is given by r=⟨t2ln⁡t,2t2+9⟩,t>0. Calculate the speed of the particle at time t=e.

a
5e
b
7e
c
5e5
d
5e
e
55e
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

First, we calculate the velocity vector v. Differentiating the position vector, we get v=drdt=⟨dxdt,dydt⟩=⟨ddt(t2ln⁡t),ddt(2t2+9)⟩=⟨2tln⁡t+t,4t⟩.

To find the velocity when t=e, we substitute in the above: v(e)=⟨2eln⁡e+e,4e⟩=⟨3e,4e⟩

To find the speed at t=e we calculate the magnitude of v(e), and we get |v(e)|=(3e)2+(4e)2=25e2=5e.

content.knowledge_point: Calculating the Speed of a Particle at a Given Time
content.problem:
The position vector $r$ of a particle $P$ (relative to a fixed origin $O$) at time $t$ is given by

$$
r=⟨{t}^{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡t,\,2{t}^{2}+9⟩,\,t>0.
$$

Calculate the speed of the particle at time $t=e.$
content.worked_solution:
First, we calculate the velocity vector $v.$ Differentiating the position vector, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}v & =\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}t} \\  & =⟨\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t},\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡t),\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2{t}^{2}+9)⟩ \\  & =⟨2t\operatorname{ln}⁡t+t,4t⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

To find the velocity when $t=e,$ we substitute in the above:

$$
\begin{aligned}v(e) & =⟨2e\operatorname{ln}⁡e+e,4e⟩ \\  & =⟨3e,4e⟩\end{aligned}
$$

To find the speed at $t=e$ we calculate the magnitude of $v(e),$ and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}|v(e)| & =\sqrt{(3e)^{2}+(4e)^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{25{e}^{2}} \\  & =5e.\end{aligned}
$$

after.name: Question 16
after.problem:
A particle $P$ moves in the $x$-$y$ plane (relative to a fixed origin $O$) with position vector

$$
r=⟨{t}^{2}{e}^{-2t},\,(t-1)^{3}⟩,\,t\in [0,\infty ).
$$

Calculate the times at which the particle is stationary.
after.worked_solution:
First, we calculate the velocity vector $v.$ Differentiating the position vector, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}v & =\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}t} \\  & =⟨\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t},\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{2}{e}^{-2t}),\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t-1)^{3}⟩ \\  & =⟨2t{e}^{-2t}-2{t}^{2}{e}^{-2t},3(t-1)^{2}⟩ \\  & =⟨2t(1-t){e}^{-2t},3(t-1)^{2}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

The particle is stationary when its velocity is zero:

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =0 \\ ⟨2t(1-t){e}^{-2t},3(t-1)^{2}⟩ & =⟨0,0⟩\end{aligned}
$$

So we need

$$
\begin{aligned}2t(1-t){e}^{-2t}=0\, & ⇒\,t=0,1, \\ 3(t-1)^{2}=0\, & ⇒\,t=1.\end{aligned}
$$

The solution $t=1$ is the only solution that satisfies both equations, so this is the only value of $t$ when the particle is stationary.

after.html:
Question 16
?

A particle P moves in the x-y plane (relative to a fixed origin O) with position vector r=⟨t2e−2t,(t−1)3⟩,t∈[0,∞).

Calculate the times at which the particle is stationary.

a
t=1
b
t=0
c
t=0,2
d
The particle is never stationary
e
t=0,1
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

First, we calculate the velocity vector v. Differentiating the position vector, we get v=drdt=⟨dxdt,dydt⟩=⟨ddt(t2e−2t),ddt(t−1)3⟩=⟨2te−2t−2t2e−2t,3(t−1)2⟩=⟨2t(1−t)e−2t,3(t−1)2⟩

The particle is stationary when its velocity is zero: v(t)=0⟨2t(1−t)e−2t,3(t−1)2⟩=⟨0,0⟩

So we need 2t(1−t)e−2t=0⇒t=0,1,3(t−1)2=0⇒t=1.

The solution t=1 is the only solution that satisfies both equations, so this is the only value of t when the particle is stationary.

content.knowledge_point: Calculating the Times at Which a Particle Is Stationary
content.problem:
A particle $P$ moves in the $x$-$y$ plane (relative to a fixed origin $O$) with position vector

$$
r=⟨{t}^{2}{e}^{-2t},\,(t-1)^{3}⟩,\,t\in [0,\infty ).
$$

Calculate the times at which the particle is stationary.
content.worked_solution:
First, we calculate the velocity vector $v.$ Differentiating the position vector, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}v & =\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}t} \\  & =⟨\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t},\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{2}{e}^{-2t}),\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t-1)^{3}⟩ \\  & =⟨2t{e}^{-2t}-2{t}^{2}{e}^{-2t},3(t-1)^{2}⟩ \\  & =⟨2t(1-t){e}^{-2t},3(t-1)^{2}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

The particle is stationary when its velocity is zero:

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =0 \\ ⟨2t(1-t){e}^{-2t},3(t-1)^{2}⟩ & =⟨0,0⟩\end{aligned}
$$

So we need

$$
\begin{aligned}2t(1-t){e}^{-2t}=0\, & ⇒\,t=0,1, \\ 3(t-1)^{2}=0\, & ⇒\,t=1.\end{aligned}
$$

The solution $t=1$ is the only solution that satisfies both equations, so this is the only value of $t$ when the particle is stationary.

$$
\begin{aligned}v & =\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}t} \\  & =⟨\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t},\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{3}-3t),\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2{t}^{2}+6t-3)⟩ \\  & =⟨3{t}^{2}-3,4t+6⟩ \\  & =⟨3({t}^{2}-1),2(2t+3)⟩ \\  & =⟨3(t-1)(t+1),2(2t+3)⟩\end{aligned}

$$

There is no value of $t$ that satisfies both equations, so there are no stationary points.

\begin{aligned}v & =\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}t} \\  & =⟨\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t},\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{3}-3t),\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2{t}^{2}+6t-3)⟩ \\  & =⟨3{t}^{2}-3,4t+6⟩ \\  & =⟨3({t}^{2}-1),2(2t+3)⟩ \\  & =⟨3(t-1)(t+1),2(2t+3)⟩\end{aligned}
$$

The particle is stationary when its velocity is zero:

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =0 \\ ⟨3(t-1)(t+1),2(2t+3)⟩ & =⟨0,0⟩\end{aligned}
$$

So we need

$$
\begin{aligned}3(t-1)(t+1)=0\, & ⇒\,t=\pm 1, \\ 2(2t+3)=0\, & ⇒\,t=-\frac{3}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

There is no value of $t$ that satisfies both equations, so there are no stationary points.
